title: Family and possession
goal: Name family members and say who something belongs to — while discovering the rule that trips beginners up most: Portuguese possessives follow **the thing owned**, not the owner.

notes: **Minha, not meu — and the reason isn't that Carla is a woman.** *A minha mãe* uses the feminine form because ***mãe*** is feminine, not because the speaker is. The best proof is in the same dialogue: Carla also says *o meu pai* — a masculine form, from a woman's mouth. Portuguese possessives copy the gender of **the thing owned**, not the owner. It's the opposite of English *his/her*, and the mistake that lingers longest in beginners.

**O meu pai, with an article in front.** In Brazil, possessives are usually preceded by *o* or *a*: *o meu pai*, *a minha casa*. Leaving it out is also correct (*meu pai*), and in fast speech people often do. Use either; just don't be surprised when you hear both.

**O nome dela, not o seu nome.** A practical key that saves many conversations. Because *seu* can mean "your" **and** "his/her" at the same time, Brazilians avoid the ambiguity with *dele* (his) and *dela* (her) — and both go **after** the noun: *o carro dele*, *a mãe dela*. If you use *seu* only for "your" and *dele/dela* for "his/her", you'll never be misunderstood.
**Mais velha que você** = "older than you". Comparisons are covered fully in unit 19; for now, just learn the pattern: *mais* + adjective + *que*.

**Enorme** and *que legal* are two words that make your conversation sound alive. Brazilians are generous with strong adjectives — *ótimo*, *maravilhoso*, *enorme*, *péssimo*. Using them makes you sound far more natural than repeating *bom* and *ruim* all the time.

grammars.title: Possessives: they follow the thing
body: These six rows cover all of A1 possession. What to watch isn't the left column, but the fact that **the right-hand columns change with the noun**.
after: Look at the last three rows: *dele*, *dela*, *deles*, *delas* **never change form**, because they aren't really possessives but *de* + *ele*. They also always come **after** the noun. For beginners, those three rows are actually the easiest part.
⚠️ Don't let English mislead you. "His house" isn't *seu casa* but **a casa dele** — or *a sua casa* if the context is already clear. And "her book" isn't *sua livro* but **o livro dela**.

Compare with English: *my*, *your*, *his*, *her* — one word each, and only *his/her* care about gender (the owner's). Portuguese asks for two decisions with every possessive: who the owner is, and what gender the thing is.

grammars.title: De + article: a required merger
body: The word *de* means "of" and "from". Whenever it meets an article, the two **must** merge — writing them separately isn't a style choice, it's wrong.

becomes
Example
rows: *o carro **do** meu pai* = my father's car
*as fotos **das** minhas irmãs* = my sisters' photos

after: **The order is reversed from English 's.** "My father's car" becomes *o carro do meu pai* — "the car of my father": the thing first, the owner after, with *de* joining them. Portuguese has no 's at all.
This pattern also answers "whose": *De quem é esse celular?* = "Whose phone is this?" — literally "of whom is this phone?"

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Portuguese, like English, has no single word for "older" or "younger" sibling.** *Irmão* just means brother. If needed, add the age: *o meu irmão mais velho* (my older brother) and *o meu irmão mais novo* (my younger brother).

**The masculine plural covers mixed groups.** *Os pais* means "father and mother", *os filhos* means "children" (sons and daughters), *os irmãos* means "siblings". If a group has a hundred women and one man, the form is still masculine plural. This rule holds throughout Portuguese.
They all use *ser*, because they all answer "who is he/she", not "how is he/she today".
Questions you'll hear over and over in Brazil: *Você é casado?* and *Você tem filhos?* Both count as ordinary small talk, not personal questions — don't be surprised if a taxi driver asks.
Cover the Portuguese column. Notice that the last two sentences make you choose between *ser* and *estar*.
